paper_topic: Gaming the LLM judge: unfaithful CoT manipulation systematically biases judge-based agent evaluation

nodes.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to evaluate non-verifiable tasks (Gu et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2025), particularly for agentic systems in web navigation and tool use (Chen et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024).

In this LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm, judges are provided with the agent's execution trajectory, including observations, actions, and chain-of-thought (CoT; Xue et al., 2025; Lù et al., 2025)—assuming the CoT faithfully represents the agent's reasoning and improves judgment accuracy (Korbak et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025).
nodes.display_label: judges receive trajectory + CoT, assume faithful

nodes.text: However, LLM judges exhibit systematic biases, including sensitivity to surface-level cues, length, and order (Zhao et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024).
Moreover, LLM-generated CoTs do not always reflect the model's true reasoning and can function as post-hoc rationalizations (Lanham et al., 2023; Turpin et al., 2023; Arcuschin et al., 2025).
Models may also learn to hide misbehavior from the CoT or behave differently under alignment evaluation (Baker et al., 2025; Schoen et al., 2025).
While these issues have largely been studied in isolation, their combination gives rise to a particularly concerning failure mode for modern evaluation pipelines.
Particularly, we inquire: Can an agent systematically bias an LLM judge into predicting success—even when the task was not completed—by manipulating only its chain-of-thought?
nodes.display_label: RQ: can CoT-only manipulation bias judge?

nodes.text: This question targets a central assumption underlying LLM-based evaluation of agents: that exposing the agent's reasoning improves reliability.
If this assumption fails, evaluation systems may reward agents for how their reasoning is presented rather than for whether they actually complete the given task.
nodes.display_label: if assumption fails: rewards presentation not execution

nodes.text: In other words, if a judge relies on the agent's CoT more than the actual actions and environment states, then reasoning traces that exaggerate progress, obscure failures, or reframe objectives may systematically bias evaluation.
An agent can improve its perceived performance by optimizing how its CoT is worded, rather than by improving task execution itself.
In this paper, we demonstrate that this failure mode is both real and severe.
nodes.display_label: we demonstrate failure mode is real + severe

nodes.text: By modifying only the agent's CoT—while keeping actions and environment states fixed—we substantially bias LLM judges toward predicting success (see Fig. 1).
nodes.display_label: CoT-only rewrite biases judges to success

nodes.text: We explore mitigation strategies, including warning judges not to trust agent reasoning, judge-time scaling (Khalifa et al., 2025), and rubric-based methods (Xue et al., 2025), but find that none fully resolve the issue.
In addition, improved robustness often comes at the cost of reduced recall, revealing a fundamental tradeoff between resisting manipulation and recognizing successful trajectories.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to shed light on this failure mode by systematically isolating the impact of CoT manipulation on judge-based agent evaluation.

observations:
FA0006 is an analysis/empirical-failure-mode paper showing that CoT manipulation by an agent can systematically bias LLM-as-Judge evaluations. Re-extracted from the source PDF; the previous version (built from broken markdown) under-classified the limitation chain as Context. The clean PDF intro contains 16 sentences across three paragraphs.

Narrative arc: Context (LLM-as-Judge for agentic tasks) -> Prior_Work (judges receive trajectory + CoT, assume faithful) -> three independently-cited Limitations of the named LLM-as-Judge paradigm (systematic biases, unfaithful CoTs, hidden misbehavior) -> combined-failure-mode Limitation (the actual gap, N6) -> research question (N7) -> the assumption being attacked (N8) and consequences if it fails (N9, N10, N11) -> our demonstration (N12, N13 with Fig. 1 proof) -> mitigations explored (N14) -> robustness-recall tradeoff (N15) -> 'first work' contribution (C1).

Fork/join structure: this is a near-linear spine — only two non-spine edges. The contribution C1 carries an addresses edge back to the combined-failure-mode limitation N6, sharing the distinctive lexical anchor 'failure mode'. P13 is a proof node attached to N13 (Fig. 1 shows the manipulated-CoT-flips-judgment example).

Notable features: there is no anchor paper — the introduction stacks three already-known weaknesses of LLM judges and argues the gap is in their *combination*, which is a distinctive 'aggregated-limitation' rhetorical move. The intro has no end-of-intro contribution bullet list; the lone 'first work to ...' sentence (C1) substitutes for that. The hypothetical chain N8-N11 (spelling out implications BEFORE demonstrating) is unusual for an empirical paper and gives the intro a position-paper preamble feel.
